items.title: World: 2025 IASC Gender Accountability Framework Report
items.author: Inter-Agency Standing Committee
items.content:
Country: World
Sources: Inter-Agency Standing Committee, UN Women

Please refer to the attached file.

UN Women and the IASC Gender Reference Group are delighted to share the 2025 IASC Gender Accountability Framework (GAF) Report.

The report provides a system-wide assessment of implementation of the 2024 IASC Policy on Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women and Girls in Humanitarian Action. It reviews progress across gender-responsive planning and implementation; meaningful inclusion, localization and financing; Gender in Humanitarian Action (GiHA) coordination; and leadership, capacity and accountability.

The monitoring exercise covered 23 humanitarian contexts and drew on consultations with 467 participants, including UN agencies, international and national NGOs, government institutions and women-led organizations (WLOs). WLOs represented the largest share of consultation participants, at 35 per cent. The process also included 120 verified cluster survey responses across 22 countries and 10 clusters.

The global report, including detailed country snapshots, identifies progress as well as persistent gaps and challenges. Key findings include:

  • Gender analysis is increasingly informing humanitarian planning: 82 per cent of HNRPs or equivalent frameworks reflected gender analysis, up from 62 per cent in 2024. However, only 23 per cent of reporting countries had at least 75 per cent of clusters monitoring programmes for the access and inclusion of women and girls and other at-risk groups, showing that important gaps remain between analysis, implementation and monitoring.
  • WLO representation in humanitarian leadership continued to expand: 87 per cent of reporting countries confirmed WLO membership in their HCTs, up from 73 per cent in 2024. Yet representation did not always translate into influence over priorities or resource allocation. Although 83 per cent of responding clusters reported WLO membership, WLOs accounted for an average of only 15 per cent of cluster members, and six of the 16 countries with cluster Strategic Advisory Groups reported no WLO representation in those bodies.
  • WLO access to Country-Based Pooled Funds improved substantially but remained uneven: WLOs made up 21.5 per cent of direct CBPF recipients, while 18 per cent of total CBPF allocations, or $189.2 million, reached WLOs, up from 11 per cent in 2024 and above OCHA’s 15 per cent global target. However, allocations ranged from 73 per cent in Venezuela, 59 per cent in Colombia and 47 per cent in Pakistan to 1 per cent in Syria, 2 per cent in the occupied Palestinian territory and Niger, and 3 per cent in Chad and the Syria Cross-Border Humanitarian Fund.
  • GiHA Working Groups remained operational across most contexts: 87 per cent of reporting countries had a functional standalone GiHA Working Group or equivalent mechanism. WLOs represented 36 per cent of GiHA Working Group membership and co-chaired half of the active groups. However, only 58 per cent had representation from at least 75 per cent of clusters, and several groups faced possible merger or restructuring under the Humanitarian Reset, creating risks to their dedicated gender coordination and accountability functions.
  • Senior gender advisory capacity increased: 83 per cent of reporting countries had such capacity for at least nine months, compared with 64 per cent in the previous cycle. Nevertheless, only 52 per cent had gender focal points in at least 75 per cent of clusters, and funding reductions and restructuring affected the availability and effectiveness of this capacity in several contexts.
  • GBV response remained critically underfunded: Only 23 per cent of HNRP countries had at least half of their identified GBV requirements funded, while 13 of 22 response plans had less than one quarter of GBV requirements funded.

The findings also demonstrate the value of the GAF as an accountability and management tool for UN Women’s humanitarian engagement. Fourteen of the 19 countries that participated in the previous cycle reported concrete action on earlier recommendations, including stronger consultation with WLOs, expanded gender focal-point networks, reforms to pooled-fund access arrangements, and new gender strategies and funding commitments.

As the Humanitarian Reset advances amid severe funding constraints, colleagues are encouraged to use the GAF findings and country-level recommendations to inform UN Women’s engagement with humanitarian leadership, coordination bodies, clusters and partners, including through in-country GiHA Working Groups or equivalent mechanisms. Priority areas include strengthening gender-responsive planning, sustaining dedicated GiHA coordination and advisory capacity, expanding meaningful WLO influence, improving equitable access to financing, and keeping commitments to gender equality and the leadership of women and girls visible and accountable throughout humanitarian decision-making.

items.title: World: COP31: FAO calls for increased funding for agrifood systems as weather extremes intensify
items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Country: World
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

In Antalya, FAO unveiled a series of reports and initiatives offering solutions as the climate crisis demands more resilient and more sustainable food production

24/11/2026

Antalya, Türkiye - Climate finance for agrifood systems is declining even as countries face increasingly severe impacts from rising temperatures and extreme weather events, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) told delegates at the 2026 UN Climate Change Conference (COP31).

Held in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026, the conference brought countries together at a defining moment in global efforts to tackle climate change and ensure food security for present and future generations.

Throughout the conference, FAO highlighted the increasing climate risks facing agriculture and food systems, including fisheries and aquaculture, and stressed the need to turn climate commitments into action. FAO underlined the urgency of action especially with the current el Niño cycle coming on top of a hotter world and likely to magnify the intensity of the anticipated droughts, extreme heat and floods.

Drawing on 41 years of satellite observations, FAO's latest analysis of projected el Niño impacts identifies major agricultural drought risks in Southern Africa, the Sahel, Central America's Dry Corridor, and parts of South and Southeast Asia, where the probability of agricultural drought exceeds 50 percent. Meanwhile, marine heatwaves have already affected 15 percent of global fisheries and have been linked to losses of 5.6 million tonnes and economic damage amounting to $6.6 billion.

The growing exposure of food production systems to climate shocks is increasingly reflected in national climate planning. According to FAO data submitted to the conference, 86 percent of countries now report the impacts of extreme and slow-onset climate events, including floods and droughts, on agrifood systems in their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). If all conditional elements of the NDCs are met, according to projections, emissions from agricultural sectors would be 41 percent lower in 2030 and 76 percent lower in 2035 than in 2019.

The vast majority of countries also recognize the potential of transforming the way food is produced, distributed and consumed to advance climate mitigation and adaptation.

At the same time, significant gaps remain in efforts to reduce emissions from degraded croplands, forest lands and grasslands, nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions from fertilizers, methane (CH4) emissions from livestock and flooded rice, and manure management.

Yet the investment needed to support the transformation of agrifood systems remains insufficient. Although food and agriculture account for 18 percent of climate finance needs, climate-related development finance for agrifood systems fell by 10 percent in 2024, the latest year for which data are available. The sectors responsible for producing food - crops, livestock, forestry and fisheries - received just 5 percent of total climate-related development finance.

“In their new climate plans countries clearly recognize the opportunities for actions that can build resilience while also reducing emissions significantly from the agricultural sector " said Kaveh Zahedi, FAO Assistant Director-General and Director of the Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment (OCB). “But the urgency for action is not being matched by climate finance, nor reflected in the negotiated outcomes”.

For countries vulnerable to climate change and fiscal pressures, grants and concessional finance remain essential to build capacity, reduce the cost of capital and make projects more attractive to future private investment, according to FAO.

FAO initiatives at COP31

Throughout the conference, FAO presented a series of reports and initiatives designed to support the members in the official discussions, help the COP31 Presidency elevate food and agriculture and offer solutions.

FAO, in close collaboration with the COP31 Presidency and the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry of Türkiye, launched the Turquoise Nexus Initiative (TNI), a country-led platform connecting food security, water management, and climate action. To ensure its sustainability, TNI will become a flagship program under the COP-to-COP Food and Agriculture (FAST) Partnership, fostering synergies with the COP29 Baku Harmoniya Climate Initiative for Farmers, and COP30's Resilient Agriculture Investment for Net Zero Land Degradation (RAIZ) Accelerator.

The FAO-hosted FAST Partnership opened COP31’s Finance Day with a Ministerial Meeting highlighting the need to scale up and improve the quality of climate finance to support farmers' adaptation and unlock the potential of agrifood systems to drive climate action. The message echoed discussions led by FAO during an official UNFCCC event on Scaling Climate Finance for Resilient Agrifood Systems Facing Extreme Heat and El Niño-related Shocks.

The vital role of young farmers was also recognized at COP31. The COP31 Youth Dialogue on Agriculture, convened on Food, Agriculture and Health Day, was co-organized by the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry, Türkiye, and FAO. The event included the presentation of the Antalya Call to Action for Youth on Agrifood Systems, led by the World Food Forum Türkiye Youth Chapter. FAO also supported the COP31 Presidency Climate Champion – a young Australian women farmer - with the new initiative Back Future Farmers: Building the Commercial Pathways for the Next Generation of Agriculture.

Another key initiative unveiled by FAO at COP31 was the Antalya Action Plan on Integrated Fire Management, a country-led, voluntary plan that aims to translate political commitments on wildfire resilience into coordinated action through greater collaboration, shared learning and expanding practical solutions.

Spearheaded by the COP31 Presidency and co-led by Brazil and the Republic of Korea, with support from FAO through the Global Fire Management Hub and from the Forest & Climate Leaders’ Partnership, the initiative was endorsed by 23 countries on Monday.

With extreme fire events projected to increase by up to 50 percent by the end of this century, the Action Plan aims to turn this consensus into practice by giving participating countries a shared community to exchange the measures they are taking to improve wildfire management, learn from one another and benefit from tools, measures and initiatives that already exist.

“The value of the Antalya Action Plan is in connecting very different experiences - from prevention and community action to technology, landscape management and international cooperation - so that countries can learn from one another and act faster,” said Zhimin Wu, FAO Assistant Director-General and Director of the Forestry Division.

Other forestry-related initiatives and events included the launch of the AFFIRM mechanism on integrated fire management; and the launch of the Peatland Breakthrough, a major new global effort to halt peatland loss, speed up restoration and unlock the finance needed to protect these important ecosystems.

Science stood at the heart of the exchanges at COP31, as Parties began discussing the next Global Stocktake, ensuring that climate action is firmly anchored in the best available evidence. Demonstrating this commitment, FAO launched simultaneously on its Platform and IPCC Platform the outcome report of the FAO–IPCC co-sponsored expert meeting on agriculture and food, which delivers critical scientific insights to bridge knowledge gaps and guide policymakers in integrating agrifood systems into effective, science-based climate solutions.

Another initiative launched in a side event seeks to address the crucial issue of financing. Bringing together six UN agencies, including FAO, the UN Disaster Risk Financing (DRF) Platform aims to secure access to more than $3 billion in risk financing to protect 75 million people and their livelihoods from potential climate shocks and natural hazards by 2030.

FAO also presented a series of publications during the conference.

On finance:

  • Climate-related development finance to agrifood systems – Global and regional trends 2026 update
  • Exploring the quality of climate finance for agrifood systems

On policy:

  • The Agrifood systems in nationally determined contributions (NDCs): A global analysis - Synthesis Report 2026
  • Mangroves for adaptation and resilience: a review of national climate plans and commitments

On Science and data:

  • FAO–IPCC co-sponsored Expert Meeting on Agriculture and Food - Outcome Report
  • Agrifood systems emissions: Global, regional and country trends, 2001–2024

On informing the negotiations:

  • Women farmers leading local climate adaptation: evidence, financing models and enabling pathways
  • Exploring the quality of climate finance for agrifood systems – An initial review
  • Measuring the food and agriculture indicators of the Global Goal on Adaptation
  • Enhancing transparency for adaptation and Loss & Damage. Technical insights from the first Biennial Transparency Report submissions
  • Beyond Koronivia and Sharm el-Sheikh: Options to advance climate action in agriculture and food security under the UNFCCC
  • Guide on post-fire restoration in Mediterranean and Near East countries
  • Tracking ecosystem-based adaptation indicators of the Global Goal on Adaptation
  • Beyond silos: Loss and damage in agrifood systems

items.title: World: El Niño and Child Rights in Africa: Assessing Risks and Strengthening Child Centred Preparedness - November 2026
items.author: Terre des hommes
items.content:
Countries: World, Ethiopia, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mozambique, Somalia, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe
Source: Terre des hommes

Please refer to the attached file.

Abstract

This paper examines the potential implications of the forecast “Super” El Niño event on children, focusing on the heightened vulnerabilities and risks in Eastern and, Southern . El Niño typically produces drought in Southern Africa and heavy rainfall and flooding in parts of East Africa, threatening agricultural production, water systems, health services, education, protection, and household livelihoods. Recent Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, (FSIN, 2026) based analysis indicates that the number of people facing crisis-level hunger or worse in six analysed countries could rise from 12.6 million to 16.4 million by March 2027, while children facing acute hunger could increase from six million to eight million. The paper recommends that child-centred anticipatory action, early warning, forecast-based financing, nutrition surveillance, resilient social services, and social protection, is essential to prevent a foreseeable climate shock from becoming a child-rights emergency.

items.title: World: Children Account for Half of Landmine Victims as Global Casualties Soar to Five-Year High
items.author: HALO Trust
items.content:
Country: World
Source: HALO Trust

24 November 2026 – Nearly 7,000 people were killed or injured by landmines and unexploded ordnance (UXO) in 2025, the highest annual toll since 2020, according to the Landmine Monitor 2026.

For the second consecutive year, children made up half of all civilian casualties for whom age was recorded, with non-combatants accounting for a staggering 84% of total recorded deaths and injuries.

Children remain particularly vulnerable to deadly explosive hazards when playing outdoors or accompanying family members working in fields and grazing livestock.

The latest findings highlight the devastating human cost of global renewed landmine use and the growing threat facing civilians returning to homes and communities contaminated by bombs.

Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties for the third consecutive year, according to the report, with 1,891 people killed or injured.

Syria, in which HALO is actively clearing landmines and UXOs, is also highlighted in the report after recording more than 1,600 casualties, a rise of more than 50% since 2024. The increase is partially driven by the return of refugees following the collapse of the Assad regime. Latest figures show that a civilian is killed or injured every six hours.

Victim-activated improvised landmines designed to detonate when a person or vehicle steps them or disturbs a tripwire, continued to cause more casualties than any other device type, accounting for 1,530 casualties last year.

Major General James Cowan, CEO of The HALO Trust, said: "Behind every statistic is a person whose life has been changed forever. It is particularly distressing that children account for half of civilian casualties. No child should have to grow up fearing that the ground beneath their feet could kill or maim them.”

The impact of a landmine explosion can last a lifetime. Survivors often face permanent disabilities, psychological trauma and years of rehabilitation, while access to healthcare, prosthetics, wheelchairs, and job opportunities remain severely limited in many affected countries.

Meanwhile, at least 65 countries and other areas were suspected or confirmed to be contaminated by antipersonnel mines or improvised mines.

items.title: World: Epidemic and emerging disease alerts in the Pacific as of 24 November 2026
items.author: Pacific Community
items.content:
Countries: World, Australia, French Polynesia (France), Micronesia (Federated States of), New Zealand, Papua New Guinea
Source: Pacific Community

Please refer to the attached Map.

Highlights/updates since the last map was sent on PacNet on 17 November 2026:

Diarrhoea

• Federated States of Micronesia – Yap State: The Yap weekly bulletin for EpiWeek 46 (09 to 15 November 2026) shows diarrhoea back at the alert threshold after two weeks below it, with 7 cases at the Yap State Hospital outpatient department against 3 in EpiWeek 45 (alert threshold 7): three children aged 3 to 5 years and four adults aged 36 to 64 years. Of two stool specimens tested, one was positive for rotavirus and one for enteroaggregative Escherichia coli. Since EpiWeek 32, the laboratory has made 137 pathogen detections in this outbreak, mostly E. coli (59) and rotavirus (40), with co-infections in 67% of confirmed patients. The blue alert for diarrhoea remains in effect for the Federated States of Micronesia (Yap State). – Source: Yap State Department of Health Services, Communicable Disease Weekly Bulletin shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 20 November 2026.

Measles

• Papua New Guinea: The National Department of Health weekly bulletins for EpiWeeks 45 and 46 (02 to 15 November 2026) report a rise in acute fever and rash cases nationally, from 11 in EpiWeek 44 to 17 in EpiWeek 45 and 24 in EpiWeek 46, above the usual weekly median. In EpiWeek 46, Gulf Province reported 16 cases, after two cases earlier in the year, followed by the National Capital District (3), Eastern Highlands (2), Hela, Madang and Manus (one each). Year to date, 505 cases have been reported and 460 samples tested, with 19 IgM-positive measles results as of EpiWeek 45. After Expert Review Group review, two measles cases (New Ireland 1, Western Highlands 1) and two rubella cases remain confirmed in 2026. The blue alert for measles remains in effect for Papua New Guinea. – Source: Papua New Guinea National Department of Health, Public Health Events Weekly Bulletins for EpiWeeks 45 and 46 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 20 November 2026.

Respiratory diseases

• French Polynesia: In EpiWeek 46 (09 to 15 November 2026), French Polynesia remained in an influenza epidemic phase, with a further increase to 142 laboratory-confirmed cases, 139 of them influenza A, and 56 hospitalisations, including seven admissions to intensive care. Two deaths were reported. Since 05 October 2026 (EpiWeek 41), 427 confirmed cases (372 influenza A), 149 hospitalisations, 13 intensive care admissions and six deaths have been recorded. Consultations for acute respiratory infection in the sentinel network remained stable, while their proportion increased. Metapneumovirus, parainfluenza 4 and rhino/enterovirus were also detected. The red alert for influenza A remains in effect for French Polynesia. – Source: Agence de régulation de l'action sanitaire et sociale (ARASS), Bulletin de Surveillance Sanitaire de Polynésie française n°41 shared with the PPHSN Coordinating Body Focal point on 24 November 2026.

• New Zealand: The laboratory-based virology weekly report for week 46 (ending 15 November 2026) records 6,018 influenza-positive specimens since 1st January 2026: 5,561 influenza A (992 A(H1N1)pdm09, 880 A(H3N2) and 3,689 not subtyped) and 457 influenza B. This is 58 more than in the week 45 report, confirming that detections continue to slow. The blue alert for influenza A remains in effect for New Zealand. – Source: PHF Science, New Zealand laboratory-based virology weekly report accessed on 24 November 2026.

Other Information:

Carbapenemase-producing Enterobacteriaceae

• Europe: On 18 November 2026, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) reported that the estimated incidence of carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae bloodstream infections in the EU/EEA reached 3.75 per 100,000 population in 2025. This is 72% above the 2019 baseline and well above the 2030 target of 2.07. ECDC rates the risk as very high for people receiving healthcare in the EU/EEA. New Delhi metallo-β-lactamase (NDM) carbapenemases are spreading, with at least one NDM-positive isolate in 84.3% of regions in 2025 against 44.7% in 2019, and carbapenemase-producing E. coli is increasingly detected in the community. Bloodstream infections with third-generation cephalosporin-resistant E. coli rose by 16.4%, and only five countries met their national targets in 2025. – Sources: BEACON, EU/EEA: Rising carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae and E. coli bloodstream infections threaten 2030 AMR targets, and Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales - fourth update accessed on 24 November 2026.

Diphtheria

• Australia: The national diphtheria update as at 16 November 2026 reports 653 cases notified in 2026, including one probable, against an average of 17 for the same period in 2022–2025. Fourteen cases were notified in the last fortnight, against 12 in the previous one: Western Australia 7, Northern Territory 5, South Australia 1 and Queensland 1, four of them respiratory. Activity remains below the peak of late May to early June 2026. Since 1st January, cases have been notified in the Northern Territory (336), Western Australia (287), South Australia (24) and Queensland (6), and all locally acquired cases belong to the same genomic outbreak group. Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people account for 95.3% of cases, and 88.9% of locally acquired cases live in remote or very remote areas. Two thirds of cases (66.3%) are cutaneous and 30.8% respiratory. A total of 120 people (18.4%) have been hospitalised, and one death was notified in April 2026. – Source: Australian Centre for Disease Control, Diphtheria in Australia, epidemiological update as at 16 November 2026 accessed on 24 November 2026.

Respiratory diseases

• Global: On 19 November 2026, the WHO Technical Advisory Group on Virus Evolution classified the SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 as a variant under monitoring, with a low additional public health risk at global level. This JN.1-lineage variant, first detected in Ontario, Canada, in May 2026, rose from 1.0% of shared sequences in week 33 to 11.6% in week 41, with 722 sequences from 18 countries as of 08 November 2026. WHO notes early wastewater signals of possible community circulation in New Zealand and Hong Kong. Antibodies induced by current vaccines still neutralise the variant. – Sources: BEACON, SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1 spreads globally via enhanced ACE2 binding while current vaccine antibodies retain neutralization and WHO TAG-VE Risk Evaluation for SARS-CoV-2 Variant Under Monitoring accessed on 24 November 2026.

Many thanks again for your continuous contributions. Please note that the alerts displayed on the map are based on information available to us as of the date of this report.

items.title: Violations of International Humanitarian Law in Lebanon: Harm Continues Despite Cessation-of-Hostilities Arrangements
items.author: Lebanon Humanitarian INGO Forum
items.content:
Country: Lebanon
Source: Lebanon Humanitarian INGO Forum

Please refer to the attached file.

November 20, 2026

Key context

The announcement of cessation-of-hostilities arrangements raised hopes for improved civilian safety and a reduction in humanitarian needs across Lebanon. However, evidence collected in the months since indicates that civilians continue to face harm, essential civilian infrastructure remains damaged or inaccessible, and humanitarian and recovery efforts continue to be affected by insecurity and restrictions on access.

Drawing on publicly available evidence, operational observations, and testimonies from NGOs working across Lebanon, this paper documents the continued humanitarian consequences of hostilities and their aftermath. It highlights concerns relating to the protection of civilians, attacks affecting civilian infrastructure and essential services, restrictions on humanitarian access, and the ongoing challenges faced by communities attempting to recover and rebuild.

These patterns continue to raise concerns regarding compliance with International Humanitarian Law (IHL), including obligations related to the protection of civilians and civilian objects, facilitation of humanitarian assistance, and accountability for alleged violations. The paper also underscores the importance of sustained international attention to the humanitarian consequences of conflict in Lebanon.

This paper, jointly issued by the Lebanon Humanitarian INGO Forum (LHIF) and the Lebanon Humanitarian and Development NGOs Forum (LHDF), builds on a previous publication released in April 2026 and reflects evidence gathered in the months since. It calls on all parties to uphold their obligations under IHL, support independent investigations and accountability efforts, protect humanitarian action, and ensure continued support to crisis-affected communities across Lebanon.

items.title: World: Local Leadership in the Age of AI: How Artificial Intelligence is Transforming Locally Led Humanitarian Action.
items.author: Humanitarian Advisory Group
items.content:
Country: World
Source: Humanitarian Advisory Group

Please refer to the attached file.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping humanitarian work in Pakistan.

This report explores how local humanitarian actors are using AI, the opportunities and risks of its adoption, and what this means for locally led humanitarian action and localisation.

It finds that while AI can strengthen local actors’ participation in the humanitarian system, it does not, on its own, shift the power, resources and decision-making needed to advance localisation.

The research was carried out by GLOW Consultants as part of the Advancing Local Leadership in Humanitarian Evidence Stewardship (ALLIES) research partnership.

ALLIES is convened by Humanitarian Advisory Group (HAG) through the Humanitarian Horizons research programme, with funding support from the Broad Reach Foundation.

items.creator: El Equipo Humanitario País Colombia
items.title: Colombia: Reporte Plan de Respuesta a Necesidades Humanitarias HNRP 2026 en el Sistema 5W entre enero y septiembre de 2026
items.author: El Equipo Humanitario País Colombia
items.content:
Country: Colombia
Sources: El Equipo Humanitario País Colombia, Grupo Interagencial sobre Flujos Migratorios Mixtos, R4V, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

Socios humanitarios continúan realizando intervenciones en diferentes regiones del país a pesar de los desafíos del contexto, en respuesta a las necesidades humanitarias que siguen agudizándose en miles de personas que habitan en territorios apartados de difícil acceso, principalmente comunidades rurales incluyendo grupos étnicos. La respuesta tiene un énfasis en asistencia humanitaria vital multisectorial, complementando las capacidades de las autoridades locales y nacionales.

  • Entre enero y septiembre de 2026 al menos 1.6 millones de personas recibieron asistencia humanitaria en 312 municipios de 31 departamentos, gracias al esfuerzo de 89 organizaciones humanitarias. De este total, el 40% de las personas atendidas son niños, niñas y adolescentes, y 26.7% pertenecen a pueblos étnicos (15,4% afrodescendientes y 11,3% indígenas).
  • El 80%de las personas asistidas (1.272.200 personas) se encuentra en zonas con necesidades humanitarias en severidad alta (4), priorizando intervenciones en asistencia alimentaria, WASH, protección, educación en emergencia. Los beneficiarios se concentran en 128 municipios de 16 departamentos de las regiones Pacífico, noroccidente, la frontera con Venezuela y Amazonía.
  • La respuesta también alcanzó a cerca de 330.000 personas en contextos de severidad moderada (2 y 3), enfocada en recuperación temprana y resiliencia comunitaria fortaleciendo la alimentación como medio de vida, acceso a servicios como salud, saneamiento básico, alojamientos y capacidades locales en otros 184 municipios de 29 departamentos, con aras de reducir vulnerabilidades. Estas acciones se han concentrado principalmente en el noroccidente, Amazonía y algunos departamentos del centro del país donde hubo concentración de necesidades por el terremoto.
  • Según los reportes, el 42% de actividades fueron implementadas por ONG nacionales y locales (incluye acciones como socios implementadores de ONGs internacionales o de agencias de Naciones Unidas); el 34% por ONGs internacionales (contempla intervenciones directas o como socio implementador de agencias UN); un 10% corresponde a intervenciones directas de agencias de Naciones Unidas, y un 14% por otros socios quienes también ejecutan acciones locales en el marco de la respuesta del Plan de respuesta del Equipo Humanitario País (HNRP 2026).
  • Gracias al apoyo de diferentes donantes, se han movilizado a la fecha USD 302,2 millones (48,8% del requerimiento total de USD 619,8 que incluye el Adenda al HNRP 2026) incluyendo USD 5 millones del CERF RR asignados en respuesta al terremoto. https://fts.unocha.org/countries/49/summary/2026
  • A la fecha, también se destaca la respuesta humanitaria complementaria para 514.000 personas (182.000 familias) con graves afectaciones por el terremoto de agosto. Las intervenciones se han llevado a cabo por parte de 42 organizaciones en 99 municipios de los 6 departamentos más afectados (Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Risaralda, Caldas y Quindío), principalmente con atención inmediata con kits de alimentos, agua, saneamiento e higiene, alojamientos con la habilitación y dotación de espacios seguros, protección, salud, entre otras actividades en el marco de la emergencia.
    Para más detalles acceder al dashboard: https://3is.org/emergenciaslatam/terremoto_choco/

Es importante garantizar la continuidad de acciones multisectoriales y el acceso humanitario de manera oportuna para mitigar las necesidades más urgentes de las poblaciones vulnerables y con doble afectación, dada la convergencia entre conflicto armado, los impactos del terremoto y otros eventos climáticos.

items.title: World: Equitable Risk Sharing in Humanitarian Action - An aspiration or an essential power-sharing arrangement? October 2026
items.author: Humanitarian Advisory Group
items.content:
Countries: World, Afghanistan, Myanmar, Pakistan, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine
Source: Humanitarian Advisory Group

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive summary

Risk sharing is ultimately a test of power and partnership. It is not demonstrated by a risk
register or a signed agreement, but by what happens when conditions change: whether
local and national organisations can raise concerns safely, influence decisions, access the
resources to adapt, and remain supported when risks materialise. This report shows how
humanitarian actors can move from transferring risk down the response chain to sharing
responsibility for safer, more effective and locally led humanitarian action.

Risk-sharing landscape

The sector has developed a growing body of frameworks, pilots and communities of practice, including the
Risk Sharing Framework, Dutch Relief Alliance pilots, the Risk Sharing Community of Practice and guidance
linking risk sharing with localisation. However, the research found few examples of fully realised, equitable
risk sharing in practice. Existing approaches remain more developed in prevention than response, and many
practices described as risk sharing are better characterised as risk management or supported risk transfer.
Donors and intermediaries often prioritise fiduciary, legal, compliance and reputational risks, while local and
national partners are more directly exposed to operational, safety, security, access, political and communitylevel
risks.

What this paper does

This paper examines how risk is currently understood, allocated and managed across humanitarian programs
and partnerships. It centres the perspectives and lived experience of local and national organisations, while
also considering the institutional perspectives of donors and intermediaries. The research covered Myanmar,
Syria, Afghanistan, Pakistan and Ukraine, with additional learning from global and multi-country initiatives.
The paper identifies emerging practices that could be strengthened and scaled, rather than presenting a set
of fully established models. It is accompanied by an Equitable Risk Sharing Playbook, which translates the
findings into practical actions across key risk categories and three phases: before, during and after a crisis.

Who this paper is for

The paper is intended for donors, intermediaries, local and national organisations, DEC members and
broader humanitarian sector. It is also relevant to program, finance, compliance, safeguarding, security and
partnership teams responsible for translating institutional commitments into operational practice.

items.content:
Countries: Yemen, Djibouti, Somalia
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Highlights

▪ Displacement in Yemen continues to rise, with more than 360,000 people newly displaced since 1 August, up from around 321,000 in the previous update. Taiz remains the most affected governorate, accounting for 64% of new displacement.

▪ Cross-border movements continue across the Gulf of Aden, with arrivals reaching 4,9191 individuals, including 4,439 arrivals in Djibouti and 480 arrivals in Somalia. During the reporting period, 115 new arrivals from Yemen were recorded in Somalia.

▪ Insecurity is driving further refugee movements within Yemen, with 4,638 refugees relocating from Kharaz camp to Aden since 7 November. An assisted spontaneous return flight to Somalia for more than 100 refugees has been postponed to 28 December.

items.author: CARE
items.content:
Country: Sudan
Source: CARE

Please refer to the attached files.

Executive Summary

Introduction and Background

CARE International (CI) operates through its Members, Candidates, and Affiliates in more than 100 countries, delivering lifesaving humanitarian assistance and long-term development support. With over 75 years of experience, CARE works to address the structural causes of poverty and inequality through a commitment to social justice, gender equality, diversity, and inclusion. The SAFER Sudan action ('Strengthening Access to Protection, Foster Care, Economic Resilience, and Reintegration') is a 48-month intervention implemented under the leadership of CARE Nederland as the Lead Applicant, in partnership with Plan International (UK), Danish Red Cross, Sudanese Red Crescent, Talawiet Organization for Development, and Child Development Foundation.

The programme is implemented across six target states: Khartoum, South Darfur, South Kordofan, Red Sea, Gedaref, and Kassala, under the European Union's NDICI–Global Europe framework. The programme adopts an integrated, multi-sectoral approach that connects protection services, family-based alternative care, child protection systems, livelihoods and economic resilience interventions, and structured pathways for social reintegration. This integrated design strengthens both immediate protection outcomes and longer-term recovery and resilience capacities within affected communities. The action is aligned with European Union priorities under the NDICI–Global Europe framework, particularly in relation to human development, social inclusion, and resilience strengthening in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

Programme Outcomes and Objectives: The SAFER Sudan programme has two main outcomes:

• Outcome 1: Increased access to safe, gender-sensitive, and age-appropriate protection services for vulnerable populations, including women, children, youth, persons with disabilities, IDPs, and survivors of gender-based violence.

• Outcome 2: Improved livelihood opportunities, with a particular focus on the equal and meaningful inclusion of the most vulnerable groups, enabling them to restore income, reduce reliance on negative coping strategies and strengthen resilience and social reintegration.

The overall objective of SAFER Sudan is to provide protection and socio-economic reintegration to at-risk groups in displacement-affected communities, through a deliberate and integrated approach that links protection outcomes with sustainable economic recovery pathways.

items.title: World Vision Launches ADH-funded Programme to Address Learning Gaps and Strengthen Child Well-being Across Eight Schools in Ukraine
items.author: World Vision
items.content:
Country: Ukraine
Source: World Vision

KYIV, 23 November – Among the children surveyed in a World Vision assessment, 90% attend school regularly and 97% have progressed to the next grade. Yet only 28% say they understand their lessons well, while 57% say some lessons are hard and 6% say most lessons are very hard.

World Vision and its local partner SpivDiia are responding with a 14-month programme funded by Aktion Deutschland Hilft e.V. The programme combines catch-up classes, psychosocial support and measures to strengthen school resilience. It will reach 5,465 children across eight schools in Dnipropetrovsk and Mykolaiv oblasts, while also contributing to stronger national systems for child protection.

“We surveyed 558 children and assessed 19 schools. What we found is that attendance does not necessarily translate into learning. Air raid alerts repeatedly force children to switch between classroom-based, blended and remote learning, disrupting their education and widening learning gaps. They need structured catch-up classes to recover what they have missed,” said Arman Grigoryan, World Vision Ukraine Crisis Response Director.

“But catching up academically is only part of the challenge. Almost half of the children we surveyed live with fear caused by bombing or shelling near their homes. It is very difficult to learn when you do not feel safe. Teachers remain children’s most trusted source of safety, yet they are under sustained strain, experiencing high levels of burnout and exhaustion. That is why this programme supports teachers and caregivers as well as children,” Grigoryan added.

Children aged 6-17 will participate in small-group catch-up classes in Ukrainian, mathematics and English, alongside history and primary-level subjects where needed, with integrated Social-Emotional Learning activities.

Adolescents aged 12-18 will benefit from First Aid Arts, an eight-session programme that uses art, movement, music and breathing techniques to strengthen resilience and emotional regulation.

Individual counselling will be provided to 300 children and 140 caregivers, while teachers and facilitators will be trained to identify children who need additional help and refer them to specialised services.

Support will extend beyond the classroom, with 600 caregivers and 200 teachers receiving training to better address children's learning and emotional needs. Teachers and psychologists will also share approaches to catch-up education and exchange experience to improve the support they provide.

To ensure that learning can continue despite power cuts and other emergencies, the programme will strengthen the resilience of eight schools through energy assessments and the provision of backup equipment, including portable charging stations, laptops and printers.

The programme will also seek to extend access to education and strengthen child protection beyond the eight participating schools. In partnership with the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine, the initiative will fund the development of online Ukrainian Language and Reading courses for primary school pupils, hosted on the national All-Ukrainian School Online platform.

At the national level, World Vision will work with the National Social Service of Ukraine (NSSU) to conduct policy-oriented research identifying gaps, barriers and opportunities in interagency coordination, children's rights protection, family-based care and cross-border child protection. The findings will inform practical recommendations and tools, while training for the NSSU's central and regional staff will support their implementation and help strengthen coordination across child protection services.

“The research will provide an evidence base on challenges in interagency coordination among child protection services, education authorities, and other stakeholders, particularly in relation to identifying children living in difficult life circumstances, detecting cases of non-enrolment or interruption of education, information sharing, and ensuring timely responses to violations of children's rights,” said Viktor Zelenyy, Director of the Department of State Control of Children's Rights Compliance at the NSSU.

“This will support us in improving the legal and regulatory framework and related procedures, developing methodological guidance and training materials for practitioners, and strengthening international cooperation on cross-border child protection,” he added.

The project runs from 1 September 2026 to 31 October 2027.

ENDS

Notes to Editor:

About World Vision Ukraine Crisis Response: World Vision Ukraine Crisis Response has supported children and families affected by the war since March 2022, reaching more than 2.4 million people, including over 1 million children, through programmes focused on education, child protection, mental health and psychosocial support, livelihoods, cash assistance, winterisation and basic needs.

For further information, please contact:

Laurentia Jora | World Vision Ukraine Crisis Response Advocacy & Communications Manager | Email: laurentia_jora@wvi.org

items.creator: UN Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen
items.title: UN Special Envoy for Yemen concludes visit to Kuwait | United Nations Peace Operations
items.author: UN Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen
items.content:
Country: Yemen
Source: UN Office of the Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Yemen

Amman, 24 November 2026 - The United Nations Special Envoy for Yemen, Hans Grundberg, concluded a visit to Kuwait, where he met with Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah.
Discussions focused on recent political and military developments in Yemen, the implications of renewed hostilities for Yemen and the wider region, and ongoing diplomatic efforts. Grundberg underscored the importance of sustained regional and international coordination in responding to the evolving situation and its political, security and economic ramifications, particularly in light of the growing pressures on the Yemeni population.

The Special Envoy expressed his appreciation for Kuwait’s sustained commitment to peace in Yemen and its support for the Yemeni people, building on a longstanding engagement in UN-led peace efforts.

During his visit, Grundberg also delivered an address at the Saud N. Al-Sabah Kuwait Diplomatic Institute to an audience of Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry officials, members of the international diplomatic community and international relations students. The address was followed by an exchange on developments in Yemen, the complexities of mediation in the current regional context and the role of diplomacy in conflict resolution.
